warmup.q: Two CPU-bound loops share one CPU. One runs at nice 0, the other at nice 10. About what share of the CPU does the nice 10 loop get?
options: About 50%: nice only matters when the system is idle
None: the nice 0 loop always runs first while it is runnable
warmup.why: The kernel turns nice 0 into weight 1024 and nice 10 into 110, and shares follow the weights: 110 / 1134 is 9.7%. In the lab box the nice 10 loop got 0.98 s of CPU in 10 s. It never gets nothing, because Linux divides time by weight instead of running strict priorities.

sections.h: One CPU, two runnable loops: the kernel has to pick
sections.html:
When I counted, the Docker VM behind the lab box had 1,055 tasks (the threads of lesson 3 of this track, from every container) and 12 CPUs. Only 9 of those tasks were ready to run. The rest were asleep, waiting on a socket or a timer. The ready ones wait in a run queue, one queue per CPU. Every few milliseconds, for every CPU, the kernel answers one question: which task runs now, and for how long? The part of the kernel that answers it is the scheduler.

Start with the simplest answer: run a task until it finishes or blocks, then run the next. That breaks the moment one task never blocks. The fraud-scorer thread from lesson 3 sits in a tight loop and never waits for anything. On one CPU, every other task, including the thread that answers your health check, waits behind it forever.

So the kernel must be able to take the CPU back from a task that doesn't give it up. Lesson 1 showed the tool: a timer interrupt. On the lab box's kernel it fires 1,000 times a second, the CPU jumps into the kernel, and the kernel may decide to run someone else. Saving one task's registers and loading another's is a context switch. With that in hand, the next simplest policy is round robin: every runnable task gets a fixed time slice, say 3 ms, then goes to the back of the line.

spin.c is a CPU-bound loop that reports how much CPU it got. Two copies pinned to the same CPU split it evenly:

pid 19 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1866 times
pid 18 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1872 times

Each was switched out about 1,870 times, so each turn lasted under 3 ms (4.99 s divided by 1,870 is 2.7 ms).

The slice length is a trade. A short slice means a waiting task gets the CPU back sooner, but every switch costs a trip into the kernel, and the next task starts with caches full of someone else's data. A long slice wastes less and makes everyone wait longer. With 3 ms slices and 30 busy tasks on one CPU, each task waits about 90 ms between turns.

Round robin's real flaw is that every task is equal. The nightly settlement batch and the authorization API get the same share of the CPU, and you have nowhere to say that one matters less.

try.title: Two loops on one CPU
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. os/c/l04/spin.c spins for the number of seconds you give it, then prints the CPU time it got and how many times the kernel switched it out.
taskset -c 0 pins a command to CPU 0, so the two copies have to share it. Predict the split before you run the third line.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/spin os/c/l04/spin.c taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 5 taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 10 & taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 10 & wait

try.expect:
PIDs and switch counts differ between runs:

pid 17 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 5.00 s (100%), switched out 319 times
pid 19 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1866 times
pid 18 nice  0: 4.99 s of CPU in 10.00 s (50%), switched out 1872 times

Alone, the loop gets the whole CPU; its few hundred switches are other work that landed on CPU 0 of your Docker VM (other containers, kernel threads). Together, each gets half, in turns of about 2.7 ms.

sections.h: nice is a weight, and fair shares follow the weights
sections.html:
Linux lets you say a task matters less with its nice value: a number from -20 to 19, where higher means "nicer to the others". Every process starts at 0. nice -n 10 cmd starts a command at 10, and renice changes a running one. Anyone can make their own process nicer. Making one less nice, more important, needs privilege (CAP_SYS_NICE) by default.

The obvious design is strict priority: always run the lowest nice value first. That starves. A settlement batch at nice 10 would get nothing while any nice 0 task is runnable, and on a busy box that can be forever. Linux wants nice 10 to mean less CPU, never none.

So the kernel turns each nice value into a weight, from a fixed table in its source:

nice -5 0 1 5 10 19
weight 3121 1024 820 335 110 15

When tasks compete for one CPU, each gets its weight divided by the sum of the weights. Nice 0 against nice 10 is 1024 / (1024 + 110): 90.3% against 9.7%. Each step in the table is about 1.25 times the next. The kernel's own comment calls that a 10% change in CPU per nice level, relative to a neighbour that stays put.

Only the ratio matters. Nice 10 against nice 15 splits a CPU the same 75/25 way as nice 0 against nice 5. And a nice 19 task alone on an idle CPU still gets all of it. Weights only decide how to divide time among tasks that all want it.

How does the kernel hand out time by weight without keeping a ledger forever? It gives each task a virtual runtime: its real CPU time, scaled by 1024 divided by its weight. A nice 0 task's virtual clock runs at real speed. A nice 10 task's clock runs 9.3 times faster (1024 / 110), so 1 ms on the CPU adds 9.3 ms to it. The rule is then one line: run the task with the smallest virtual runtime. Heavy tasks have slow clocks, stay behind, and get picked more often, exactly in proportion to their weights. That rule was the heart of CFS, the Completely Fair Scheduler, which Linux used from 2.6.23 (2007) until 6.6.

The lab box agrees with the arithmetic. Nice 0 against nice 10 on one CPU:

pid 16 nice  0: 9.01 s of CPU in 10.00 s (90%), switched out 1381 times
pid 17 nice 10: 0.98 s of CPU in 10.00 s (10%), switched out 364 times

try.title: Nice 0 against nice 10
steps: In the box, start one loop at nice 0 and one at nice 10, both on CPU 0. Predict the split from the weights 1024 and 110.
Halfway through, ps shows the nice value (NI) and the CPU share each one has had so far.
Then change 10 to 5 and predict again.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/spin os/c/l04/spin.c taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 10 & taskset -c 0 nice -n 10 /tmp/spin 10 & sleep 5; ps -o pid,ni,pcpu,comm -C spin wait

try.expect:
PID  NI %CPU COMMAND
   16   0 89.8 spin
   17  10  9.5 spin
pid 16 nice  0: 9.01 s of CPU in 10.00 s (90%), switched out 1381 times
pid 17 nice 10: 0.98 s of CPU in 10.00 s (10%), switched out 364 times

90.1% and 9.8%, against the 90.3% and 9.7% the weights predict. With nice 5 one run gave 7.53 s and 2.47 s: 75/25, as 1024 / (1024 + 335) says. The nice 0 loop's switch count moves a lot between runs, because other work on CPU 0 also switches it out. The nice 10 loop's count stays near 350.

sections.h: EEVDF: being owed time makes you eligible, the earliest deadline runs
sections.html:
"Smallest virtual runtime first" gets the shares right, but it says nothing about when. Every task gets the same slice. A thread that wakes up to answer a 2 ms API call waits behind a batch job's full slice, and a task can't say "I want short turns, often". CFS handled it with heuristics around wake-ups. Linux 6.6 began replacing it with EEVDF, Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First, and 6.12 finished the move. The lab box runs 6.12.

EEVDF keeps virtual runtime and adds two ideas.

The first is lag: how far a task is behind or ahead of its fair share. The kernel keeps V, the weighted average of every runnable task's virtual runtime: where each task would be if the CPU had been shared perfectly. A task at or behind V has lag zero or more. It is owed CPU time, and it is eligible. A task ahead of V has had more than its share, and it waits, however urgent it looks.

The second is the virtual deadline. Each time a task starts a slice, the kernel sets a deadline: its virtual runtime plus the slice converted to virtual time, slice × 1024 / weight. Among the eligible tasks, the one with the earliest deadline runs. A task that asks for 1 ms slices gets an earlier deadline than one with 3 ms slices, so it runs sooner and more often, for less time each turn. Its share stays the same; its waiting shrinks.

The default slice is 0.75 ms × (1 + log2 of the number of CPUs, counting at most 8). That's 3 ms on any machine with 8 or more CPUs, including the lab box. Since 6.12 a task can ask for its own slice with sched_setattr().

One consequence surprises people. A nice 10 task doesn't get shorter turns. It gets a full 3 ms slice every time it runs, but its deadline sits far ahead in virtual time, so its turns come rarely. In the nice 10 run above, the loop ran 0.98 s in 364 turns: 2.7 ms each.

The stepper runs the first slices for a nice 0 task and a nice 5 task, with the real numbers.

try.title: Read a task's turns from /proc
steps: /proc/<pid>/schedstat has three numbers for a task: nanoseconds on a CPU, nanoseconds waiting in a run queue, and how many turns it got.
Start the nice 0 and nice 10 loops again, read both files after 5 s, and work out the average turn length for each loop: time on CPU divided by turns.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/spin os/c/l04/spin.c taskset -c 0 /tmp/spin 6 & a=$! taskset -c 0 nice -n 10 /tmp/spin 6 & b=$! sleep 5 cat /proc/$a/schedstat /proc/$b/schedstat wait

try.expect:
4506153596 495090551 489
488818878 4507422520 190
pid 17 nice  0: 5.41 s of CPU in 6.00 s (90%), switched out 547 times
pid 18 nice 10: 0.59 s of CPU in 6.00 s (10%), switched out 225 times

The nice 10 loop ran 0.49 s in 190 turns, 2.6 ms per turn: one slice of about 3 ms each time, as EEVDF promises. It spent 4.5 s waiting. The nice 0 loop averaged 9.2 ms per turn, often several slices in a row, because it stayed eligible with the earliest deadline. The middle number, time spent runnable but waiting, is the one to watch when you suspect a CPU is overloaded.

sections.h: A CPU quota is a budget per 100 ms, and spending it early means stalling
sections.html:
Everything so far divides CPUs among tasks that compete for them. A container needs something else: a ceiling. A pod with a CPU limit of 0.5 must not use more than half a CPU, even when the node is idle. Weights can't do that, because a task alone on a CPU gets 100% whatever its weight.

So cgroups, the groups of processes from lesson 3 that carry the pids limit, have a second CPU control: a budget. The file cpu.max holds two numbers in microseconds, a quota and a period. docker run --cpus=0.5 writes 50000 100000: the group may use 50 ms of CPU time in every 100 ms period. When the budget runs out, the kernel stops every thread in the group until the next period starts. That is throttling. Kubernetes CPU limits work the same way; its documentation says "cpu limits are enforced by CPU throttling".

The budget is CPU time, not CPUs. Four busy threads on four CPUs spend 50 ms of CPU time in 12.5 ms of wall time, then all four wait about 87 ms. To a request handler that looks like the JVM froze. CpuQuota.java runs busy threads and records every gap over 10 ms:

50000 100000
availableProcessors() = 1
4 busy threads for 2.1 s used 1.0 s of CPU
stalls over 10 ms: 92, longest 94 ms
nr_periods 41
nr_throttled 40

cpu.stat counts it. nr_periods counts the periods that passed while the group was busy, and nr_throttled the ones in which it ran out of budget: 40 of 41. A bigger limit doesn't change the shape. --cpus=2 with the same four threads gives a 200 ms budget, spent in 50 ms, followed by 50 ms of nothing. That run still saw 81 stalls, the longest 59 ms.

The JVM reads cpu.max when it starts and sizes itself from it. availableProcessors() returned 1 under --cpus=0.5 (it rounds up) and 2 under --cpus=2. With one CPU the JVM picks the Serial garbage collector instead of G1, and it sizes compiler threads, the common ForkJoinPool and the virtual-thread carriers from the same number. The quota never limits how many threads you run, though. Every extra busy thread spends the budget faster and makes the freeze longer.

There is a second way to give a container two CPUs. --cpuset-cpus=0,1 lets it run only on CPUs 0 and 1, with no budget at all. The same four threads got the same 4.0 s of CPU, and only 2 stalls over 10 ms. The comparison below has both runs.

Half a CPU's worth of time: 1.0 s in 2 s. The longest stall is close to a whole period, because the four threads spend the 50 ms budget early and then wait out the rest. With --cpus=2 you should see 200000 100000, availableProcessors() = 2, 4.0 s of CPU and still dozens of stalls (81 in one run, the longest 59 ms).

refs.title: Control Group v2: the cpu controller (cpu.max, cpu.stat)
Kubernetes: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

analogy: Think of one espresso machine shared by an office. Round robin is everyone pulling one shot in turn. Weights are the rule that the on-call team pulls about nine shots for every one the interns pull, and nobody is ever locked out. EEVDF adds a fairness check at the front of the queue: only people who've had less than their share may step up, and among them, whoever needs the machine for the shortest time goes first. A CPU quota is a prepaid card that resets every 100 ms: once the team's card is empty, the whole team waits for the reset, even if the machine is idle. The analogy breaks at the virtual clock. People in an office remember who had coffee. The kernel keeps no history at all, only one number per task, its virtual runtime, and the average of those numbers says who is owed.
world: Your authorization service runs in a pod with a 2-CPU limit on a 32-core node. The JVM reads cpu.max, reports 2 processors and sizes its garbage collector, its ForkJoinPool and its virtual-thread carriers for 2 CPUs. Vert.x under Quarkus sizes its event loops from the same number. But the pod also runs a Kafka consumer pool and a JDBC pool, so during a burst 12 threads are runnable at once. They spend the 200 ms budget in under 20 ms, and every thread in the pod freezes for the rest of the period. The card issuer's 120 ms call is fine; your own p99 can jump by up to 80 ms with no GC log entry to explain it. Check /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat before you tune the heap: if nr_throttled climbs with nr_periods, the limit is the cause. For latency-sensitive services, give the pod a CPU request and either no CPU limit or one with headroom over the burst, and keep busy-thread counts close to the budget.
mistake: Reading a CPU limit of 2 as two CPUs. It's 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, spent by however many threads are runnable at once. Eight busy threads spend it in 25 ms, and then the whole container waits 75 ms. People size thread pools to the limit and watch an average CPU graph that sits at 60% of the limit, which looks healthy, while every busy period ends in a stall. The averages hide it because a stall costs no CPU. The fix starts with measuring: compare nr_throttled with nr_periods in cpu.stat. Then either cut the number of threads that burn CPU at the same moment or raise the budget. A smaller gotcha with the same flavour: on a Linux desktop, two loops started from two different terminals ignore each other's nice values. Each terminal is its own session, autogrouping puts each session in its own group, and nice only ranks tasks within a group.

compare.title: Two CPUs' worth of time against two whole CPUs, with four busy threads

a.label: --cpus=2 (a quota)
a.title: CpuQuota 4 2
a.html:
200000 100000
availableProcessors() = 2
4 busy threads for 2.0 s used 4.0 s of CPU
stalls over 10 ms: 81, longest 59 ms
nr_periods 25
nr_throttled 22

b.label: --cpuset-cpus=0,1 (a CPU set)
b.title: CpuQuota 4 2
b.html:
max 100000
availableProcessors() = 2
4 busy threads for 2.0 s used 4.0 s of CPU
stalls over 10 ms: 2, longest 13 ms
nr_periods 0
nr_throttled 0

compare.note: Both containers got 4.0 s of CPU in 2 s, and the JVM reported 2 processors in both. The quota let all four threads run at once on four CPUs, so they spent each period's 200 ms in 50 ms and then sat throttled for the other 50. The CPU set gave no budget, only two CPUs, so the scheduler shared them among the four threads in 3 ms slices and nobody waited more than a few slices. Same total, very different worst case. A latency-sensitive service cares about the worst case.

worked.title: Find out whether a pod's latency spikes come from throttling

steps.say: Read the budget from inside the container. Two numbers in microseconds: quota, then period. max means no limit.
steps.code: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max # 200000 100000 -> 200 ms of CPU time every 100 ms: a limit of 2 CPUs

steps.say: Read the counters twice, a few seconds apart, under real traffic. The ratio of the two deltas is the share of periods in which the group ran out of budget.
steps.code: grep -E 'nr_(periods|throttled)' /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat; sleep 10 grep -E 'nr_(periods|throttled)' /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat # nr_periods 25 / nr_throttled 22 in the --cpus=2 demo: throttled in 88% of periods

steps.say: Check what the JVM believes, because it sizes its thread pools from this. -XshowSettings:system prints the container settings the JVM detected.
steps.code: java -XshowSettings:system -version 2>&1 | head -6 # Operating System Metrics: # Provider: cgroupv2 # Effective CPU Count: 1 # CPU Period: 100000us # CPU Quota: 50000us

steps.say: Count the threads that want CPU at the same time. R in the stat column means running or runnable. If that number is well above the quota in CPUs, each period's budget goes in a fraction of the period. Fix it by cutting busy threads (smaller pools, fewer GC threads with -XX:ParallelGCThreads) or by raising the limit, then read cpu.stat again to confirm nr_throttled stopped climbing.
steps.code: ps -L -p $pid -o tid,stat,pcpu,comm | awk '$2 ~ /^R/' | wc -l

lab.title: Build a scheduler simulator: round robin, weighted fair, EEVDF
steps: Open spin-nice.txt. It is real output of this lesson's spin.c in the lab box: three pairs of loops on one CPU, at nice 0 against 10, 5 and 0. The tests compare your simulator with these numbers.
Read Scheduler.kt top to bottom. The weight table, Task, Timeline and Cpu.run are written for you. Cpu.run asks the scheduler for a task, runs it for sliceFor(task) ms, calls charge, and repeats.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All eight fail.
Write WeightedFair.pick and charge. The test that compares with the lab box should now pass: 90/10, 75/25 and 50/50.

Write Eevdf.eligible, pick and charge. The stepper's order, A B A A A B, is one of the tests. The last test shows a task with a 1 ms slice waiting at most 3 ms for its turn while still getting only a third of the CPU.
hints: tasks[next++ % tasks.size] is a whole round robin.
minBy returns the first of several equal minimums, which is the tie-break the tests expect.
EEVDF's pick is filter then minBy. The filtered list is never empty: the task with the smallest virtual runtime is always at or behind the weighted average.
In Eevdf.charge, compare with a little slack (task.vruntime >= task.deadline - 1e-9). Floating point makes 3.0 come out as 2.9999999999999996.

drill.title: Weights, virtual time and the EEVDF pick, from memory
drill.prompt: Write the three lines at the core of EEVDF: how a task's virtual runtime grows, which tasks are eligible, and which eligible task runs. Then write what cpu.max holds for --cpus=0.5.

answer.html: // after a task runs ms of real time task.vruntime += ms * 1024 / task.weight // nice 0 = 1024, nice 10 = 110 // eligible: owed time, at or behind the weighted average V val v = tasks.sumOf { it.weight * it.vruntime } / tasks.sumOf { it.weight } val eligible = tasks.filter { it.vruntime <= v } // earliest virtual deadline wins; deadline = vruntime + slice * 1024 / weight val next = eligible.minBy { it.deadline } // --cpus=0.5 -> /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max = "50000 100000": 50 ms of CPU time per 100 ms

recap: The scheduler picks which runnable task runs on each CPU and for how long. A timer interrupt lets it take the CPU back; a context switch hands it over.
nice -20 to 19 maps to a weight (nice 0 = 1024, nice 10 = 110). Competing tasks share a CPU in proportion to their weights; nice 0 against nice 10 is 90/10.
Virtual runtime is real CPU time × 1024 / weight. EEVDF runs the eligible task (virtual runtime at or behind the weighted average) with the earliest virtual deadline.
The default slice is 3 ms on 8 or more CPUs. A task with a shorter slice waits less between turns without getting more CPU. /proc/<pid>/schedstat shows time on CPU, time waiting and turns.
cpu.max is a budget, not a CPU count: 50000 100000 is 50 ms per 100 ms. Busy threads spend it early and the whole group is throttled until the next period; cpu.stat counts nr_throttled.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our pod has a 2-CPU limit and the dashboard says it averages 1.2 CPUs, so CPU can't be why p99 jumps by 60 ms." Explain what the limit really is and how it can still be the cause.
explain.answer: The 2-CPU limit isn't two CPUs. It's a budget in cpu.max: 200 ms of CPU time every 100 ms period, shared by every thread in the pod. The node has many CPUs, so when traffic bursts, ten threads can run at once on ten CPUs and spend the whole 200 ms in about 20 ms of wall time. Then the kernel throttles the pod: no thread runs until the next period starts, up to 80 ms later. Any request in flight just stalls. Averaged over a minute, usage is still well under the limit, because stalled time costs no CPU, so the dashboard looks fine. The proof is in cpu.stat: if nr_throttled rises along with nr_periods, we're being throttled. We can fix it by having fewer threads burn CPU at once, for example smaller pools, or by raising or removing the limit while keeping the CPU request for placement.

deeper.html:
Linux 6.12 also merged sched_ext: a scheduler class whose policy is a set of BPF programs loaded at run time. If the BPF scheduler misbehaves or stalls a task, the kernel drops it and moves every task back to the fair scheduler, EEVDF. You can't try it in the lab box. Docker Desktop's kernel is built without it:

$ zcat /proc/config.gz | grep SCHED_CLASS_EXT
# CONFIG_SCHED_CLASS_EXT is not set

On a distribution kernel built with it, /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state says whether a BPF scheduler is loaded, and the kernel tree's tools/sched_ext has example schedulers such as scx_simple.

The fair scheduler doesn't only weigh tasks. It weighs groups. Every cgroup has a cpu.weight (default 100, range 1 to 10000), and CPU is first divided among sibling groups by their weights, then among the tasks inside each group by nice. That's why nice doesn't cross container boundaries: a nice 19 loop in one container and a nice 0 loop in another split the CPU by the containers' weights. Autogrouping does the same for terminal sessions on a desktop (/proc/sys/kernel/sched_autogroup_enabled is 1 in the lab box too).

Sleep is the case this lesson's busy loops never hit. In CFS, a task that slept a long time came back with a small virtual runtime and could hog the CPU, so CFS moved waking tasks forward to near the minimum. EEVDF handles it with lag. A task that goes to sleep stays on the run queue for a while, marked for "deferred dequeue" in the kernel docs, and its lag decays, so a long sleeper eventually comes back with its lag reset.

For pressure across many tasks at once, read PSI, the pressure stall information files: /proc/pressure/cpu for the whole machine and cpu.pressure in each cgroup. In the lab box the first one read some avg10=5.78: over the last 10 seconds, at least one task was waiting for a CPU 5.78% of the time. That's run-queue waiting, the same thing the middle number of schedstat measures for one task.

sources.title: sched_ext: extensible scheduler class (Linux kernel documentation)
